core_conclusion: Under matched prompts, tools and per-system compute, whether multi-agent coordination helps is governed mainly by the single-agent baseline: above an empirical capability-saturation threshold of roughly 45% single-agent accuracy, adding agents is unlikely to improve performance. Across 260 configurations (6 agentic benchmarks x 5 architectures x 3 LLM families) the multi-agent effect spans +80.8% to -70.0% with an overall mean of 0.0%, and decomposability rather than difficulty determines when coordination pays. The threshold matched the sign of the multi-agent effect in 94% of 16 validation configurations; the fitted 20-parameter model reaches cross-validated R2 = 0.373 (0.413 with a task-grounded capability index) and picks the best architecture in 87% of held-out configurations, but leave-one-dataset-out R2 = -2.09 confines it to within-domain selection.
why_it_matters: Replaces the 'more agents is all you need' heuristic with a controlled experiment and a usable decision rule for architecture selection; shows sequential interdependence rather than task difficulty moderates coordination benefit; quantifies the coordination tax (turns scale as 2.72(n+0.5)^1.724, hybrid uses 6.2x the turns of a single agent, error amplification rises from 1.0 to 17.2); and is unusually disciplined about which effects survive cluster-robust inference.
why_nature: A corrective, field-shaping result for the multi-agent hype cycle, delivered with an experimental-science protocol (260-cell factorial, matched compute, three vendor families, five topologies); supplies mechanism via trace-derived coordination metrics and a MAST failure taxonomy, not just measurement; applies cluster-robust SEs, VIF diagnostics, bootstrap CIs and LODO validation while explicitly labelling non-surviving effects; and offers immediately deployable guidance plus a full open-source and Zenodo release.
